content: Splinter hemorrhages are small areas of bleeding that occur beneath the fingernails or toenails. These hemorrhages appear as thin, red to reddish-brown lines of blood under the nails, aligned in the direction of nail growth. They are referred to as splinter hemorrhages because their appearance resembles a splinter lodged under the nail. In certain medical conditions, particularly infective endocarditis, blood clots can dislodge from an affected heart valve and travel to various parts of the body. When these clots reach the fingers, they can damage the capillaries, leading to the formation of splinter hemorrhages. Splinter hemorrhages are a nonspecific clinical finding and may be associated with several conditions, including antiphospholipid syndrome, Janeway spots, psoriatic nails, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, subacute bacterial endocarditis, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), trauma, and trichinosis. The causes of splinter hemorrhages, listed alphabetically, include cholesterol embolization, endocarditis, psoriatic nails, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), trauma, trichinosis, and vasculitis. Initially, splinter hemorrhages appear plum-colored but darken to a brown or black hue over the course of several days. The presence of splinter hemorrhages is not a highly sensitive finding but is relatively specific for the diagnosis of endocarditis. Only about one in six patients with endocarditis will exhibit splinter hemorrhages. Therefore, the absence of splinter hemorrhages does not rule out endocarditis. However, if there is clinical suspicion of endocarditis and splinter hemorrhages are observed, this finding is considered fairly specific for the condition. During a physical examination, particular attention may be given to the heart and circulatory system to assess for underlying conditions that could contribute to the development of splinter hemorrhages.
